newsitem.title: UK: Major rules out naming election date this week.
newsitem.headline: Major rules out naming election date this week.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Thursday dampened speculation that he was about to announce the date of Britain's election as a new opinion poll showed his Conservative party badly trailing Tony Blair's Labour party.
There had been intense speculation that Major might name the date at or before the ruling Conservatives' semi-annual conference this Friday and Saturday in Bath, western England.
But in an interview with the Western Daily Press, a regional newspaper, Major said: "There will be no announcement at or before Bath. I am not going to speculate beyond that."
Most politicians expect voting to take place on May 1, but Major refused to put an end to the guessing game or even say whether he would name the day next week.
"I am not going to give any indication one way or another," he told the newspaper.

The last legally possible date for the election is May 22 but Major has said it would definitely be no later than May 1 -- the date of local elections in England -- leaving him just seven weeks to rescue the dismal fortunes of his struggling party.
A new survey of voting intentions released on Thursday illustrated the mountain the Conservatives must climb if they are to win their fifth consecutive election.
The poll, by Opinion Research Business for bookmakers Ladbrokes, showed Labour had widened its lead to 24 percentage points from 19 in the firm's previous poll two months ago.
Support for Labour, in opposition since 1979, rose to 53 percent from 51, while backing for the Conservatives slipped to 29 percent from 32.
With other polls showing a similarly wide lead for Labour, Blair has been warning his supporters against complacency.
"Though many people may write off the Tories, and take the voters' verdict for granted, I for one do not," he said on Wednesday.
In recent days, the Conservatives have unveiled a raft of policies designed to convince voters that they have not run out of steam and deserve a fifth successive term of office.

Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell on Wednesday annnounced plans that would virtually end the role of local councils in running homes for the elderly, leaving the job to commercial organisations and voluntary bodies.
Other recent initiatives have included a plan to reduce the state's role in pension provision by letting workers use tax breaks to purchase cover for their old age.
But the government's efforts to revive Conservative fortunes have been hit by a spate of controversies.

Allegations that a failure to enforce inspection standards at abattoirs was putting Britons at risk of exposure to lethal bacteria forced Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg on Wednesday to make his second statement to parliament within a week.
The ruling party was also hit by a report on Thursday that parliament's Education Committee had slammed a new government initiative for a voucher system for nursery schooling.
The upsets appeared to leave the political initiative with Labour, which under Blair has shed many of its traditional socialist policies and moved to the political centre.
